title: Myrcene Terpene: Aroma, Effects and the Mango Myth
h1: Myrcene Terpene: Aroma, the Mango Myth and What Research Shows
metaDescription: What is myrcene? How common it is in cannabis, its aroma, where else it occurs, the mango myth, what sedation research shows and how to find it on labels.
excerpt: Myrcene gives many strains their earthy, musky aroma and a reputation for heavy, relaxed highs. Here's what research actually shows, from the mango trick to lab results.
keyTakeaways: Myrcene is one of the terpenes found at the highest average levels in U.S. cannabis, and it's also common in hops, lemongrass and bay.
The mango trick doesn't add up: one analysis estimated it would take well over a thousand mangoes to approach a gram of myrcene.
Sedation findings come mostly from animal studies using doses far above what cannabis delivers.
Human research on myrcene is nearly absent, so its link to couch lock remains unproven.
Michigan labels don't have to list terpenes, so check the package, the product listing or the producer's lab data.
body:
The myrcene terpene, also called beta-myrcene, ranks among the most abundant aroma compounds in cannabis and a big part of the earthy, musky smell of many strains. It's also behind some of cannabis culture's most repeated claims, from eating a mango first to blaming myrcene for couch lock. Here's what myrcene is, where it shows up and what research does and doesn't support.

## What the myrcene terpene is

Myrcene is a monoterpene, one of the smaller, more volatile members of the terpene family. Plants make terpenes for aroma and defense, and cannabis makes them in the same resin glands, called trichomes, that produce cannabinoids. The form found in cannabis is beta-myrcene, and lab reports often list it that way.

Myrcene isn't known to produce a high on its own. In a 2022 study of cultured brain cells, myrcene at concentrations a cannabis user might realistically reach didn't change signaling at the CB1 receptor, the main target of THC. Outside cannabis, it occurs naturally in foods and drinks, from hop-forward beers to citrus.

## How common beta-myrcene is in cannabis

Very common. A 2022 study of terpene data for about 43,000 flower samples from six U.S. states found that myrcene, beta-caryophyllene and limonene were present at the highest levels on average. The researchers sorted the samples into three chemical groups, and every group included samples where myrcene outranked most other terpenes. Most CBD-dominant and balanced THC-and-CBD samples were myrcene-dominant.

Highest doesn't mean high, though. Any single terpene rarely makes up more than about 1% of a flower's weight, compared with THC levels of 10 to 20% or more.

## Smell and taste

Myrcene smells earthy, musky and herbal, with a mildly sweet flavor, and it's a familiar note in hops. In a strain, it usually blends with other terpenes, which is why two myrcene-forward strains can still smell quite different. Paying attention to that blend is a simple way to learn which aromas you enjoy.

## Where else myrcene occurs

You've met myrcene outside cannabis many times. It's a major part of hop oil, making up as much as 70% of the essential oil in some hops, and it shows up in lemongrass, verbena, bay and citrus fruits. Mangoes contain it too, but in tiny amounts: one analysis put mango levels at roughly 0.09 to 1.29 mg per kilogram of fruit.

## Mangoes and myrcene: myth vs. evidence

The idea, popular among some cannabis consumers, is that eating a mango shortly before a session makes the high stronger, supposedly because of the fruit's myrcene. The numbers don't support it. Researchers ran the numbers using 1 mg of myrcene per kilogram of mango and about 200 grams of fruit per mango. By their math, it would take well over a thousand mangoes to approach a single gram of myrcene. For comparison, an ounce of a high-myrcene strain baked into brownies would hold around 400 mg.

The mechanism looks shaky too, since myrcene didn't change CB1 signaling in that 2022 lab study, and no clinical evidence backs the trick. Enjoy the mango as a snack, but don't count on it to change your dose.

## Traditional uses: lemongrass tea

Lemongrass, a plant that contains myrcene, is one of Brazil's most popular folk remedies, traditionally brewed as a tea for its supposed calming effects. Brazilian researchers put that tradition to the test in the 1980s. In a double-blind study of 50 volunteers, lemongrass tea did no better than a placebo on how quickly people fell asleep, how well they slept, dream recall or waking during the night. In a second test with 18 people prone to anxiety, the tea didn't lower anxiety either. The tradition is interesting history, not evidence.

## What research explores: sedation, pain, inflammation and antioxidant activity

Most myrcene research happens in lab dishes and animals. A 2021 review found reports of anti-anxiety, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and pain-related activity, mostly from animal and cell studies. It counted only two human studies, both involving inhaled plant oils with less than 25% myrcene, and concluded that human data are lacking.

- **Sedation.** In a 2002 mouse study, injected myrcene at 100 to 200 mg per kilogram of body weight reduced activity, relaxed muscles and lengthened drug-induced sleep. At the higher doses, it nudged anxiety-related behavior up, not down.
- **Pain and inflammation.** Animal and cell studies report effects, but no studies show that myrcene relieves pain or inflammation in people.
- **Antioxidant activity.** These are lab findings, so far without human trials behind them.

Dose matters here. Converted from mice to people by body surface area, the standard method for comparing doses across species, 100 mg per kilogram works out to roughly 570 mg for a 70-kilogram adult, given by injection. A typical joint, about a third of a gram of flower at roughly 1% myrcene, holds about 3 mg.

The research cuts both ways. In two-year studies by the U.S. National Toxicology Program, male rats given very large oral doses of myrcene developed kidney tumors, and male mice developed liver tumors. Reviewers note those doses were roughly 100,000 times higher than typical exposure from flavorings in food, and they question how well the results apply to people. The FDA has said myrcene poses no public health risk at its intended flavoring use, but because of those animal results it stopped allowing synthetic myrcene as an added food flavoring in 2018. Either way, isolated myrcene isn't a proven supplement.

## Myrcene and couch lock: what is known

Couch lock is the heavy, sink-into-the-sofa feeling some strains are known for, and myrcene often gets the blame. Some reviews repeat a cutoff of about 0.5%, with strains above it said to feel sedating and strains below it more energetic. Here's what's actually known:

- The sedation evidence comes from animals given large injected doses, not from people using cannabis.
- Human studies of myrcene are close to nonexistent, so the 0.5% cutoff hasn't been tested in controlled trials.
- Myrcene shows up across chemical groups, and indica and sativa labels don't reliably match a product's chemistry.

THC dose and tolerance are better-understood influences on how heavy a session feels. Our guides to [indica strains people choose at night](/blog/indica-strains-for-sleep/) and the [entourage effect](/blog/the-entourage-effect/) cover how other compounds may fit in.

## Finding myrcene on labels and lab results

Michigan labels must show THC and CBD content and the testing lab, plus the harvest date where it applies, among other details, but terpenes aren't on the required list. Some producers add them anyway, on the package, in an online product listing or in a lab report.

When you find a terpene panel:

- Look for beta-myrcene or β-myrcene, usually given as a percentage or in milligrams per gram.
- Check whether myrcene is the top terpene or one of several.
- Note the total terpene number for a sense of how aromatic the product is.
- Use the harvest date as a freshness cue, since terpenes fade over time.

If a label doesn't list terpenes, ask your budtender whether the producer publishes lab data. Our guide to [reading a cannabis label](/blog/how-to-read-a-cannabis-label/) walks through every line. Our overview of [cannabis terpenes](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/) covers myrcene's neighbors, including [linalool](/blog/linalool-terpene/) and [humulene](/blog/humulene-the-earthy-terpene/).

faq.a: Earthy, musky and herbal, with a mildly sweet flavor. It's a major part of the aroma of hops, so the note may feel familiar. In cannabis, myrcene usually blends with other terpenes, so the same amount can smell different from one strain to the next. The product's terpene panel, when there is one, shows what it's paired with.

faq.q: Does eating a mango make you higher?
faq.a: There's no good evidence it does. Mangoes hold only tiny amounts of myrcene, about 0.09 to 1.29 mg per kilogram of fruit in one analysis, so you'd need well over a thousand mangoes to approach a gram. In a lab study, myrcene also didn't change the CB1 signaling that THC acts on. Enjoy the mango as a snack.

faq.q: Is myrcene the reason some strains feel sleepy?
faq.a: It's possible but unproven. High doses of myrcene sedated mice in a lab study, yet people take in far smaller amounts from cannabis, and human studies of myrcene are nearly nonexistent. THC dose and tolerance are better-understood reasons a session can feel heavy, and indica labels don't reliably predict a product's chemistry.

faq.q: How do I find myrcene on a label?
faq.a: Look for a terpene section on the package or the product listing, where myrcene may appear as beta-myrcene or β-myrcene, usually as a percentage. Michigan doesn't require terpenes on labels, so some products won't list them. If yours doesn't, ask your budtender whether the producer publishes lab data.

review.summary: 32 claims checked: 28 ok, 4 fixed (0 wrong, 1 unsupported, 3 overstated); 1 ok claim got a precision edit (NTP tumors by sex and species). Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links; research described as animal and cell findings, no pain, sedative or anticancer claim as fact.

claims.source: Sommano et al. 2020, Molecules: monoterpenes are the 10-carbon class; trichomes "are the localization of the cannabinoids and the terpenes"; terpenes "responsible for the defense and interaction with herbivores and pests" https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7763918/ ; Surendran 2021 ("monoterpene")

claims.claim: "Myrcene doesn't produce a high on its own"

claims.claim: 2022 cultured-neuron study: at concentrations users might realistically reach, myrcene didn't change CB1 signaling (body, mango section, FAQ)

claims.claim: "Outside cannabis, it's a common flavoring and aroma ingredient in foods and drinks"
claims.fix: now "it occurs naturally in foods and drinks, from hop-forward beers to citrus"; the NTP paragraph adds that FDA stopped allowing synthetic myrcene as a food flavoring in 2018 (outdated for the U.S. as of October 2026)

claims.claim: Any single terpene rarely exceeds about 1% of flower weight, vs THC at 10-20% or more
claims.source: Dvorakova 2022: "Levels of a given terpenoid in cannabis are low (seldom exceeding 1%) and far lower than levels of THC (10–20% or more)"; Smith 2022: individual terpenes "rarely present at more than 0.5% weight"

claims.claim: Smell: earthy, musky, herbal; familiar note in hops (excerpt, body, FAQ)
claims.source: Surendran 2021: "scent notes that are spicy, earthy and musky"; hop odour "herbaceous, resinous, green, balsamic, fresh hop"; Sommano 2020: "musky or hop-like fragrance"

claims.claim: Up to 70% of the essential oil in some hops; also in lemongrass, verbena, bay and citrus (body, takeaway 1)
claims.source: Surendran 2021: "can constitute as much as 70% of the essential oil by volume" (hop essential oil); "hops, cannabis, lemongrass, verbena and bay ..., as well as in citrus fruits and citrus juices"

claims.claim: Mango myrcene roughly 0.09 to 1.29 mg/kg (body, FAQ)
claims.source: Dvorakova 2022: "Levels of myrcene in mango vary considerably (0.09–1.29 mg/kg)"

claims.claim: At 1 mg/kg and ~200 g per mango, well over a thousand mangoes to approach 1 g of myrcene (body, takeaway 2, FAQ)

claims.claim: An ounce of a high-myrcene strain baked into brownies holds around 400 mg
claims.source: Dvorakova 2022: "1 oz (28 g) of this strain into a brownie recipe, this would yield ~400 mg of myrcene" (1.42% strain)

claims.source: Dvorakova 2022: myrcene "popularly supposed to be the active ingredient underlying the 'mango effect'"; Surendran 2021: two human studies only, none on this

claims.claim: Lemongrass, which contains myrcene, is one of Brazil's most popular folk remedies, used as a tea for supposed calming effects
claims.source: Leite et al. 1986 abstract: "lemongrass, one of the most popular Brazilian herbal medicines, used for its alleged CNS-depressant effects" https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2429120/ ; Surendran 2021 (lemongrass)

Few studies conducted in humans (n = 2) ... inhaling plant essential oil extracts containing <25% of β-myrcene"; "studies conducted in humans is lacking"

claims.claim: "A 100 mg per kilogram dose would mean about 7 grams of myrcene for a 70-kilogram adult" (compared with ~400 mg in an ounce)
claims.fix: rewritten: mouse doses don't transfer pound for pound; by body-surface-area scaling 100 mg/kg in mice is about 8.1 mg/kg, roughly 570 mg for a 70 kg adult (by injection), versus about 3 mg in a typical joint (0.32 g at ~1% myrcene). The 7 g figure overstated the gap about 12-fold

claims.fix: none (still true after dose scaling: ~570 mg equivalent vs ~3 mg per joint)
claims.source: do Vale 2002; FDA 2005 Table 1; Dvorakova 2022

claims.fix: precision: kidney tumors in male rats, liver tumors in male mice

claims.source: Kesner & Lovinger 2020 (THC effects and tolerance) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7388834/ ; myrcene human data lacking (Surendran 2021)

review.notes: Writer: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links. No anticancer, pain or sedative claims as fact; the NTP finding is presented with the review's caveats. No strain names (the Dvorakova strain is described only by its myrcene level). Arithmetic: 100 mg/kg x 70 kg = 7 g. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 32 claims, 4 fixed. The 7 g line applied a mouse mg/kg dose to a person one-to-one; FDA body-surface-area scaling gives about 570 mg, compared now with ~3 mg per joint. 'Common flavoring' was outdated for the U.S. (FDA delisted synthetic myrcene in 2018, 83 FR 50490). 'Hint of ripe fruit' unsupported. 'Doesn't produce a high' softened. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): Smith et al. 2022 (PLoS One, PMC9119530, full text re-read through NCBI efetch) analyzed 89,923 samples, but only 42,843 had terpene data; its terpene, chemotype and label findings rest on that subset (the label comparison is "in terms of terpene profile"), so the sample count in this article now names the subset. R 420.504(1)(c) reads "Date of harvest, if applicable" (Cornell LII copy read 2026-10-24; law-facts mi-labeling), so the label line now says the harvest date appears where it applies.

writerClaims.claim: n = 89,923 flower samples; myrcene among the top three on average; myrcene across clusters; CBD-dominant and balanced samples mostly myrcene-dominant; labels don't match chemistry.

Monoterpene; hops up to 70%; lemongrass, verbena, bay, citrus; flavoring agent; reported activities mostly animal; two human studies; 0.5% couch-lock cutoff repeated; NTP tumors; doses five orders of magnitude above food exposure.
Mango effect; mango 0.09-1.29 mg/kg; well over a thousand mangoes; ounce of 1.42% strain about 400 mg; terpenoids seldom over 1%; no CB1 effect at 1 µM; 100 mg/kg for muscle relaxation.
Mice 100 and 200 mg/kg i.p.: reduced activity, muscle relaxation, longer barbiturate sleep; slight anxiogenic effect.
Lemongrass tea: 50 volunteers, no hypnotic effect; 18 anxious subjects, no anxiolytic effect.
Michigan labels: THC and CBD, testing lab, harvest date; terpenes not required.
